---
title: "Deeplearning Evaluation Metrics"
---

The metrics themselves (accuracy, precision, recall, AUROC...) are mostly identical math. What changes in deep learning is the *framework around* the metrics. Let me give you the map.

## The one idea that reorganizes everything: loss ≠ metric

In traditional ML you often optimize and evaluate with closely related things. In deep learning, two distinct quantities live side by side:

```
   LOSS                      METRIC
   ─────                     ──────
 What the model            What humans
 optimizes during          actually care
 training (must be         about (can be
 differentiable)           non-differentiable)

 e.g. Cross-Entropy        e.g. Accuracy,
      Dice Loss                 Dice score, AUROC

        │                        │
        ▼                        ▼
  Guides gradient          Judges quality;
  descent, updates         reported in papers,
  weights every step       used for model selection
```

Why split them? Because the thing you care about (e.g. "did we classify the tumor correctly") is often a *step function* — flat gradients, useless for backprop. So you train on a smooth surrogate (cross-entropy) but *judge* on the real metric (accuracy, Dice, etc.). A model can have decreasing loss yet a metric that plateaus — and that gap is itself diagnostic information.

## The landscape, organized by task

This is the part that's genuinely broader than traditional tabular ML. Deep learning spans many task types, each with its own metric family:

```
TASK              TYPICAL METRICS
────              ───────────────
Classification    Accuracy, Precision/Recall,
                  F1, AUROC, AUPRC, confusion matrix
                  → same as traditional ML

Segmentation      Dice (F1 for pixels), IoU/Jaccard,
                  Hausdorff distance
                  → core to medical imaging

Object detection  mAP (mean Average Precision),
                  IoU thresholds (e.g. mAP@0.5)

Regression        MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²
                  → same as traditional ML

Generation        FID (images), BLEU/ROUGE (text),
                  perplexity (language models)
```

For your world specifically, segmentation and detection metrics (Dice, IoU, mAP) are where deep learning adds the most that's *new* relative to classical ML — they measure spatial overlap, not just label correctness.

## The third axis: you watch metrics *over time*

In traditional ML you often get one final score. In deep learning, evaluation is temporal — you track loss and metrics across training epochs on separate splits:

```
score
  │      val metric (what we select on)
  │     ╱‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾  ← plateaus / dips = overfitting
  │    ╱
  │   ╱___________  train metric (keeps rising)
  │  ╱
  └──────────────────────► epochs
```

The *gap* between train and validation curves is how you read overfitting, underfitting, and when to stop training. This continuous monitoring discipline is a defining feature of DL evaluation that barely exists in simple traditional ML workflows.

---

So the broad picture: **same metrics, three new lenses** — (1) loss vs metric separation, (2) a much wider menu organized by task type, (3) metrics tracked across training, not just at the end.
